problems.problem: There is no persisted keyring_serial floor, so the keyring is replayable. The keyring is fetched from the licence server on every catalogue call (§1.3 step 3) and verified only against pinned ROOT_KEYS — which an OLD keyring also satisfies. A compromised store, a MITM, or anyone who can bind the loopback override host (§2.8 step 1) serves the pre-revocation keyring, and a revoked/stolen K_release becomes trusted again. This destroys the single stated recovery from K_release theft (T3; §7 row "K_release compromised ... customers pick it up on the next catalogue call") — i.e. the one control standing between release-key theft and permanent RCE on every customer.
problems.evidence: Spec §2.7 defines the floor F over release serials only (`F = max(J.floor, max to_serial over done operations)`). §2.11 enumerates state.json contents as "serial, floor, per-module archive_sha256/tree_sha256/version" — keyring_serial is absent. §2.8 step 2's verification order lists keyring signature → json.loads → strict schema, with no serial-floor step. S3 acceptance (§9) nonetheless requires a test for "`keyring_serial` below the floor", so the intent exists but the data model never stores the value it compares against. UNVERIFIED in any container (Docker daemon unavailable: npipe dockerDesktopLinuxEngine missing) — this is a spec-internal contradiction, verifiable from the spec text alone.
problems.fix: Persist `keyring_serial` in state.json AND in an `hm.store.operation`-derived DB floor (highest wins, same pattern as the release floor), and refuse any keyring whose serial is below it — before the release index is even looked at. Add the refusal to §2.8 step 2 as an explicit ordered step, and add `keyring_serial` to the §2.11 `done` write. Ship the bootstrap with the floor pre-seeded from the keyring it carries.

problems.problem: hm_store updates itself through the store, and ROOT_KEYS lives inside the self-updated tree, so K_release can overwrite the root of trust. `lib/trust.py` is an ordinary file in the hm_store archive; "Update all" plans every installed store module and hm_store is always entitled. One release signed with a stolen K_release therefore ships a `trust.py` pinning attacker-chosen ROOT_KEYS, after which K_root can no longer revoke anything on that customer — the vendor has no path back. §4.2 step 3's builder guard runs on the vendor's own builder and is irrelevant to an attacker who holds the signing key.
problems.evidence: §1.1 C7 places trust.py at `addons/hm_store/lib/trust.py`, inside the module tree; §1.2 row K_release says it signs "**all code**"; §2.2 states hm_store is "downloadable and installable for any valid, unrevoked licence" and §1.4 step 5 plans every installed store module whose archive_sha256 differs. §4.2 step 3 places the only ROOT_KEYS check in the builder (`tools/build_release.py`), not in the client. §2.10 rule 5 validates the staged manifest's version/auto_install/installable/license/depends but never the contents of trust.py. UNVERIFIED against a container; derived from the spec text.
problems.fix: Break the circularity: either (a) require a K_root co-signature on any release whose hm_store archive changes `lib/trust.py`, checked client-side before the swap; or (b) move ROOT_KEYS out of the updatable tree into a file written once at bootstrap under a path hm_store refuses to overwrite, with the running trust set compared against it; or (c) at minimum make §2.10 refuse an hm_store archive whose trust.py root set is not a superset of the currently trusted one unless a higher-serial K_root keyring authorises the change. Add this as an S3/S5 acceptance test.

problems.problem: The entire trust chain roots in an emailed SHA-256 fetched from an unspecified vendor HTTPS host, which breaks invariant 1 for every new installation. The bootstrap zip carries ROOT_KEYS; nothing signs it. The two "channels" are a vendor web host and vendor email — both vendor infrastructure, and the spec never requires the bootstrap host to be separate from store.hushmand.tech / license.hushmand.tech, nor requires DKIM/DNSSEC, nor publishes the K_root fingerprint anywhere an operator could check independently. An attacker who compromises vendor mail or the vendor web host substitutes the bootstrap and owns every subsequent install — no key theft required. Invariant 1 ("A total compromise of the server ... yields denial of service and data exposure, never remote code execution") is therefore false for the install path.
problems.evidence: §1.2 last table row: "Bootstrap zip — vendor HTTPS + SHA-256 in the licence email (two channels) ... trust on first use, once". §1.5 steps 1-2 have the operator check the hash from the email and unzip straight into the addons data dir. §9 S10 says only "a bootstrap zip published on the vendor's HTTPS host" — one host, unnamed. D5 (§10) separates the store hostname from the licence hostname but says nothing about the bootstrap host. No signature over the bootstrap zip appears anywhere in §4.3 `bootstrap`. UNVERIFIED in container; spec-internal.
problems.fix: Sign the bootstrap zip with K_root (not K_release) and publish the K_root fingerprint on a channel the vendor does not control end-to-end (printed in the contract, in the signed quote PDF, read aloud on the onboarding call). Make §1.5 step 1 verify the K_root signature, not a hash. State explicitly that the bootstrap host must not share credentials, TLS key, or DNS zone control with the store/licence hosts, and record the compromise-of-mail case in the §5 threat table — it is currently absent.

problems.problem: K_licence is stored unencrypted on disk and the spec leaves it that way, on the same machine and directory as the new K_release. §4.1 specifies `BestAvailableEncryption(getpass())` only for the new root and release keys; the existing licence key generator writes a plaintext PKCS8 PEM and the loader cannot even accept a passphrase. D6's "never in one backup with K_licence" addresses backups, not the live filesystem — one laptop compromise yields K_release (RCE on every customer) and K_licence (mint any licence, defeating T24 whichever way require_registration is set).
problems.evidence: E:\web\hushmand-odoo\tools\issue_license.py:74 — `encryption_algorithm=serialization.NoEncryption()`; :101 — `serialization.load_pem_private_key(path.read_bytes(), password=None)`; :56 — `DEFAULT_KEY_PATH = pathlib.Path.home() / ".hushmand" / "licence_signing_key.pem"`. Spec §1.2 gives K_release custody as "C1, passphrase-encrypted PKCS8 `~/.hushmand/release_signing_key.pem`" — the same directory. §4.1 lists `--generate-root` and `--generate-release` only; no migration of the existing key is specified anywhere in the spec or in slice S5.
problems.fix: Add to S5: re-key K_licence to a passphrase-encrypted PEM (`BestAvailableEncryption`), teach `load_private_key` a `--passphrase`/getpass path, re-issue outstanding licences under the new key, and rotate VENDOR_PUBLIC_KEY in hm_license.py:56 plus `config/odoo_store.php`. Until that lands, treat T24/D9 as offering no protection and flip `require_registration` to true at first sale rather than "within the first month".

problems.problem: The "offline release station" is not offline, and the one human check on what gets signed has a bypass flag. §4.2 step 1 requires `gh run list --commit <sha>` — an outbound call to GitHub — and a git worktree of a fetched tag, on the machine holding K_release and K_licence. A network-connected signing host is the concrete precondition for the K_release theft that findings 1 and 2 make unrecoverable. Separately, step 8's typed confirmation `sign release 3` is the only point where a human reads the per-module diff sheet before a signature is produced, and `--yes` skips it, so a compromised build script signs arbitrary content silently. D8 explicitly forbids an override for the CI-green check but leaves one on the human review.
problems.evidence: Spec §1.1 C1: "Offline release station (vendor laptop, full-disk encrypted, no inbound)" — "no inbound" is not offline. §4.2 step 1: "if CI is not green for that commit (`gh run list --commit <sha> --json conclusion`)". §4.2 step 8: "require the typed confirmation `sign release 3` (or `--yes`)". §10 D8: "checked automatically by the builder ... with no override flag". UNVERIFIED in container; spec-internal.
problems.fix: Split the pipeline: an online build/verify host produces the artefact set and the CI attestation, which is carried to a genuinely air-gapped signer that only hashes, displays the review sheet, and signs. Remove `--yes` entirely, or restrict it to a `--dry-run`/no-key mode. Record in D6 that K_release must never sit on a host that runs `gh`, `git fetch`, or a browser.

problems.problem: The `licence` envelope field is never verified or bound to `payload_b64`/`sig`, yet it is the rate-limit key. §3.3 explicitly says the envelope "is not inspected at all — the envelope is carried only for the hash and the audit trail". Since limits are keyed on sha256 of that unauthenticated, attacker-chosen string, anyone holding one valid (payload_b64, sig) pair gets a fresh limiter bucket per request simply by varying the `licence` field. Both per-licence limits (`odoo-catalogue` 6/min, `odoo-archive` 60/min) collapse to the per-IP limits alone, which a stolen-key attacker distributes trivially. This also makes `key_sha256` — a UNIQUE column and the audit join key — attacker-controlled rather than a stable licence identifier.
problems.evidence: Spec §3.3 step 4 (envelope not inspected); §3.6 "Rate limits ... keyed on `sha256(whitespace-stripped licence)`"; §3.2 `$t->char('key_sha256', 64)->unique();`. The spec reproduces the existing flawed pattern verbatim: E:\web\hushmand-license-server\app\Providers\AppServiceProvider.php:19-25 keys `license-api` on `hash('sha256', $request->input('license_key'))`, i.e. on unverified request input. Note also that hm_license canonicalises on verify (E:\web\hushmand-odoo\addons\hm_license\models\hm_license.py `_decode`: `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",",":"))` over the *parsed* object), so one licence has unlimited valid envelope encodings even without tampering.
problems.fix: Key every Odoo limiter on `payload.licence_id` extracted AFTER `sodium_crypto_sign_verify_detached` succeeds (verify first, then throttle; use a cheap pre-verify per-IP limit to bound signature work). Drop the `licence` field from the request entirely — it carries no authenticated information — and derive `key_sha256` from `payload_b64` instead, or replace it with `licence_id` as the unique key.

problems.problem: Registration does not constrain entitlement, so it is a much weaker control than T24 claims. Authorisation reads `payload.modules` and `payload.expires` from the presented licence and never compares them to the registered `odoo_licences` row, whose `modules`, `expires_on` and `max_databases` columns are written once at registration and then used for nothing. An attacker holding K_licence (see finding 4 — it is stored in plaintext) forges a licence carrying a *known, registered* `licence_id` with `modules` = every module and `expires` = 2099, and `require_registration = true` lets it straight through. licence_ids are not secret: they appear in the offline bundle filename, in `odoo_store_events.licence_id`, and on the customer's own hm.license record.
problems.evidence: Spec §3.4 step 2 looks up by `licence_id` and checks only `status`; step 3 tests `today(UTC) > payload.expires`; §3.5 archive tests `module ∈ payload.modules ∪ always_entitled` — all three read the presented payload, none reads the stored row. §3.2 defines `odoo_licences.modules`, `expires_on`, `max_databases` with no consumer. §5 T24 asserts "`require_registration = true` means an unregistered `licence_id` gets no downloads, whatever it is signed with" — true, but silent on the registered-id reuse case. §6 names the bundle `hushmand-19.0-r<serial>-<licence_id8>.hmpkg`, leaking the id. UNVERIFIED in container; spec-internal.
problems.fix: In `OdooStoreService::authorise()`, after signature verification, compare the presented payload against the registered row and reject on any divergence (`modules`, `expires`, `max_databases`, `customer`) with a distinct code such as `licence_mismatch`, logging it as a probable forgery. Authorise from the stored row, not the presented payload. Add an S6 acceptance test: a correctly-signed payload with a registered licence_id but a widened `modules` list is refused.

problems.problem: `database_uuid` is client-chosen, so the activation limit — the stated server-side control for licence-key theft — does not limit a thief at all. A single attacker holding a stolen key picks one uuid and reuses it forever: step 4 refreshes the existing activation and consumes no further slot, so downloads are unlimited and the only trace is a changing `last_ip` in an events table nobody watches. The limit constrains the number of distinct *honest* installs, not the number of unauthorised downloads. The spec itself concedes the uuid "is an accounting label, never a credential", but then lists "server activation limit" among T11's controls.
problems.evidence: Spec §3.6: "`database_uuid` is an accounting label, never a credential (it is world-readable to any logged-in Odoo user via `/web/session/account`)". §3.4 step 4: "an `active` row refreshes `last_seen_at`, `last_ip`, versions". §5 T11 control column: "... server activation limit, registration, revocation, event log". §5 "Deferred" defers installation keypairs and proof-of-possession on the stated ground that "none of them prevents remote code execution" — which is true but is not what T11 is about. UNVERIFIED in container; spec-internal.
problems.fix: Either state plainly in T11 that the activation limit is accounting, not a theft control, and accept it; or pull proof-of-possession forward: on first activation the client generates a keypair, registers the public key against (licence_id, database_uuid), and signs subsequent requests — the deferral rationale does not apply to T11. In the interim add cheap detection: alert on an activation whose `last_ip` ASN changes, or whose archive-download count exceeds the module count by a wide margin, and surface it in `odoo:activations`.

problems.problem: No cap on the catalogue HTTP response body, so a MITM or compromised store can exhaust a worker's memory before any signature is checked. The caps enumerated in §2.8 apply to the *documents* (keyring 64 KiB, release.json 2 MiB, archive 20 MiB) but the keyring and index arrive base64-encoded inside a single JSON body that the client must fully read and `json.loads` to reach them. `requests` also transparently decompresses `Content-Encoding: gzip`, so a small response expands without bound. This is reachable by threat T4 (network attacker), for whom the spec otherwise claims "integrity comes from signature + hash" — true for integrity, but availability is not covered, and invariant 1's "denial of service" allowance is about the *licence server*, not about a network attacker killing the customer's Odoo.
problems.evidence: Spec §2.8 step 1 specifies `stream=True` for the transport but the archive is the only object with a described streaming cap (step 3: "stream to `downloads/<m>.zip.part`, abort past `archive.size`"). Step 2 goes straight to "unknown `key_id` → refuse" with no body-size handling. The caps sentence lists per-document limits only. No `Content-Length` check, no decompression limit, and no `max_content_length` appears anywhere in §2.8 or §1.1 C8. UNVERIFIED in container; spec-internal.
problems.fix: Cap the catalogue response: reject on `Content-Length` > 4 MiB, then read via `iter_content` with a hard byte ceiling and abort past it, before `json.loads`. Either set `Accept-Encoding: identity` or count decompressed bytes against the same ceiling. Add negative tests to S3/S7: an oversize response, and a gzip bomb.

problems.problem: There is no freshness signal on the online path, so a compromised or MITM'd store silently pins a customer to a stale release forever. Nothing in the client requires the index to be recent, and the floor rule (§2.7 step 1) guarantees only that the serial never goes *down*. An attacker who holds the store — or sits on the network — simply keeps returning the release serial the customer already has, and the "Check for updates" button reports "up to date" indefinitely. Security fixes never arrive and nobody is told. The spec recognises exactly this risk for offline media and warns on `created_at` older than 180 days, but the online path, which is the default, has no equivalent.
problems.evidence: Spec §6 step 5: "`created_at` older than 180 days shows 'This bundle is old; security fixes may be missing'". §1.3 steps 3-4 and §2.7 step 1 contain no age or freshness check for the online index; §2.7 step 1 only handles `S < F` (downgrade) and `S == J.serial` ("up to date"). §5 "Deferred" drops "server-signed freshness (`K_ts`)" on the ground that it does not prevent RCE. Invariant 1 characterises server compromise as yielding "denial of service" — but silent denial of security updates is not the visible DoS that framing implies. UNVERIFIED in container; spec-internal.
problems.fix: Apply the offline rule to the online path too: warn on the Store screen and in the check-and-notify cron (D13) when the verified index's signed `created_at` is older than N days, and again when the last successful catalogue call is older than N days. Both are a few lines and need no new key. Reconsider `K_ts` once the keyring floor (finding 1) exists — a signed timestamp is the same verification path.

problems.problem: The status route is unauthenticated, unthrottled, and selects its database from a client header, so it is a free DoS amplifier and a database-name oracle. Every request performs a database lookup against `hm.store.operation` keyed on a token hash. Nothing in the spec rate-limits it, and `X-Odoo-Database` lets an anonymous caller enumerate which databases exist and which have hm_store installed by differential response. It is the only `auth='none'` surface hm_store adds, and §2.4 justifies its existence carefully without bounding its abuse.
problems.evidence: Spec §2.4: `@http.route('/hm_store/status/<string:token>', type='http', auth='none', methods=['GET'], csrf=True, save_session=False)` and "The client sends `X-Odoo-Database: <db>` to select the database without a session ... and `credentials: 'omit'`". No rate limit, no cap on request frequency, and no mention of failing identically for an unknown database. §2.4's threat discussion covers CSRF and free-text leakage only. Odoo's own behaviour when a bad database is named is UNVERIFIED (Docker daemon unavailable).
problems.fix: Return an identical 404 with a constant-time-ish path for unknown token, unknown operation and unknown/absent database, so nothing distinguishes them. Add a per-IP limit in front of the route, and make the route a no-op (404) once the operation reaches a terminal state and the token is cleared. Verify the unknown-database behaviour in S1 acceptance 6, which currently probes only the happy path.

problems.problem: The first-time-setup runbook is ordered so that step 2 cannot succeed, and the natural operator workaround is a permissions mistake. Step 2 tells the operator to unzip into the addons data dir; step 3 is the `chmod 700` that makes it writable. Odoo creates that directory at mode 0500, so the unzip in step 2 fails with EACCES even for the owning user. Operators who hit that will reach for `sudo unzip` (leaving root-owned trees the odoo user cannot later swap, breaking invariant 5) or `chmod 777` (widening the blast radius T23 exists to contain).
problems.evidence: Spec §1.5: step 2 "As the odoo user, unzip `hm_license/` and `hm_store/` into the addons data dir", step 3 "Run **one** command ... `chmod 700 /var/lib/odoo/addons/19.0`". §1.1 C10 and §2.6 check 5 both state the directory is created 0500 and needs manual +w. The mode-0500-blocks-owner-write behaviour is standard POSIX but UNVERIFIED in the odoo:19 image (Docker daemon unavailable).
problems.fix: Swap steps 2 and 3, and have §2.6 check 5's message and STORE-INSTALL.md show chmod first. Add to S10's runbook acceptance an explicit check that no step requires root and that the placed trees are owned by the odoo user; have preflight check 5 also fail when the data dir or its children are not owned by the Odoo process uid, which catches the `sudo unzip` outcome.

problems.problem: Full unencrypted database dumps are written and retained with no stated file mode or deletion guarantee. The dumps contain every payroll, HR and financial record in the customer's database — for ministry customers, the most sensitive data on the box. `pg_dump` creates the output file under the process umask (commonly 0644); only the 0700 work directory protects it, and that protection is asserted once at creation (preflight check 6) and never re-checked. §2.11 says backups are kept for "the last 2 operations and the last 2 pg_dumps" but no actor is named as responsible for deleting older ones, and the failure paths (§7) leave dumps behind indefinitely.
problems.evidence: Spec §2.8 step 4 describes the detached `pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner` writing `<store_dir>/backups/<db>-<op>.dump` plus a `.done` JSON, with no mode specified. §2.6 check 6 creates the work dir `0700` but there is no re-check. §2.11 states the retention intent; §7's failure rows do not mention dump cleanup. §2.10 specifies 0640/0750 for placed module files but says nothing about backups. UNVERIFIED in container.
problems.fix: Open the dump target with an explicit 0600 fd and pass it to pg_dump; re-assert the 0700 mode on the work dir in preflight rather than only at creation. Name the pruning owner (the reconcile in §2.11) and prune on the failed and stalled paths too. State in the wizard text that the dump contains the full database unencrypted and where it lives, so operators can include it in their own retention policy.

problems.problem: S2's acceptance test for removing the committed admin password checks only the working tree, so the credential survives in git history and in every existing clone and deployment. `git grep` searches the checkout, not `git log -S`. The constant is also likely baked into deployed vendor directories and into any production database row created by the seeder, neither of which the acceptance covers. Since the spec gates sending customer licence blobs to the server on S2 landing, the gate is weaker than it reads.
problems.evidence: E:\web\hushmand-license-server\app\Support\LicenseDefaults.php:9 — `public const ADMIN_PASSWORD = 'Farhad@P@ssw0rd@1161997';` (plaintext, committed). Spec §9 S2 acceptance (a): "`git grep` for the old default password finds nothing". Confirmed adjacent hygiene gaps: .env.example:4 and :16 both set `APP_DEBUG=true`; .env.example:9 ships an empty `LICENSE_SIGNING_SECRET=`, which is the seeder-silently-generates path §3.8 flags.
problems.fix: Change acceptance (a) to `git log -p -S'<password>' --all` returning nothing, which forces a history rewrite or an explicit accepted-risk note; and add (f): the production admin password is rotated to a value that has never been in the repository, verified by logging in with the old one and being refused. Keep the §3.8 ordering — no customer licence blob reaches the server until this lands.

verdict:
Do not proceed to implementation as written. The spec's security engineering is unusually thorough at the layer it concentrates on — the unpack rules (§2.10), the verify-before-parse ordering, the refusal to ever disable TLS verification, the release-serial floor, and the no-free-text error model are all correct and better than most of what ships in this category. The failures are not in that layer; they are in the two places the design treats as settled and therefore never tests: key lifecycle and server-side authorisation.

Three are blockers, and they compound into one story. There is no persisted keyring_serial floor, so an old keyring can be replayed and a revoked release key becomes trusted again (finding 1). hm_store updates itself and ROOT_KEYS lives inside the tree it updates, so one K_release-signed release can overwrite the root pin and cut K_root out permanently (finding 2). And the whole chain is bootstrapped from an emailed SHA-256 over an unspecified vendor HTTPS host with no signature and no independent fingerprint (finding 3). Together these mean the spec's central promise — invariant 1, that code is authorised only by an offline key and a server compromise never yields RCE — does not hold for new installs, and that K_release theft, which §7 presents as a recoverable event, is in fact unrecoverable. The signing-key handling underneath makes this worse rather than better: the existing licence key is written with NoEncryption() at issue_license.py:74 and left that way, in the same directory as K_release, on a "release station" that §4.2 step 1 requires to call out to GitHub, with the one human review of what gets signed bypassable via --yes.

The server-side majors are a separate cluster and cheaper to fix: the `licence` envelope is never bound to the payload it accompanies yet is the rate-limit key (finding 6, reproducing the flawed pattern already live at AppServiceProvider.php:19-25); registration records entitlement columns that authorisation never reads, so T24's protection is narrower than claimed (finding 7); the activation limit is presented as a theft control but does not constrain a thief at all, because database_uuid is client-chosen (finding 8). Two availability gaps round it out: an uncapped catalogue response body reachable by a network attacker before any signature check (finding 9), and no freshness signal on the online path, so a held store can silently starve a customer of security updates while reporting "up to date" (finding 10) — the spec applies exactly this check to offline bundles and omits it from the default path.

Recommended sequencing: fix findings 1, 2, 6, 7 and 9 in the design before S3 begins, since each changes code that S3's own acceptance tests must cover; resolve finding 3 and the key-custody items (4, 5) before the first bootstrap zip is published, which is before S10 and arguably before S2; and either implement or explicitly downgrade the T11 claim (finding 8) rather than shipping a control table that overstates what the server does. Findings 10 through 14 are small and can ride along.

One caveat on evidence: the Docker daemon was unavailable during this pass (npipe dockerDesktopLinuxEngine missing) and no Odoo source exists on this disk, so I verified nothing against Odoo 19 itself. Every Odoo-runtime claim in the spec — Appendix A in full, and the starred items especially — remains unverified by me and is untouched by this review; the findings above are spec-internal contradictions or are cited to lines I read in the two Hushmand repos. S1 remains correctly placed as the slice that can kill the project, and nothing here argues against running it first.
